lead: Thermoplastics soften when heated and harden when cooled, so they can be shaped again and again. Injection moulding melts plastic pellets and forces the melt into a closed mould, cycle after cycle, to make discrete parts such as phone cases, bottle caps and car trims. Extrusion pushes the same melt through a die without a closed mould, giving a continuous pipe, film or profile. The key idea is the same: heat the polymer until it flows, shape it, then cool it below its softening point. Cooling, not filling, usually sets the production rate.
prereq: You need: the basic idea of force and pressure; the sheet-metal chapters on bending and deep drawing are useful analogies for tooling, but polymer melt flow is new.

sections.h3: Polymer melt and the injection moulding machine

blocks.text: A polymer is a long-chain molecule made by joining many small units called monomers. A thermoplastic is a polymer that softens on heating and can be remelted; examples are polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene and ABS. A thermoset is a polymer that cures into a cross-linked network and cannot be remelted; examples are epoxy and phenolic resin. The melt is the hot, flowable polymer. Viscosity is its resistance to flow: high viscosity means a thick, slow-flowing melt.

items: Barrel and screw: heaters melt the pellets; the rotating screw mixes and conveys the melt.
Nozzle: connects the barrel to the mould and injects the melt.
Mould: contains the cavity that gives the part its shape; the clamp holds it closed.
Injection unit: stops screw rotation and pushes the screw forward as a ram.
Fill: the screw moves forward and melt fills the mould cavity.
Pack: pressure is held while the cooling part shrinks, so more melt enters.
Cool: water channels in the mould remove heat until the part is stiff enough.
Eject: the mould opens, ejector pins push out the part, and the clamp closes for the next cycle.

blocks.where: t<sub>c</sub> is cycle time in seconds; t<sub>fill</sub> is fill time; t<sub>pack</sub> is pack or hold time; t<sub>cool</sub> is cooling time; t<sub>eject</sub> is ejection and mould-reset time.

sections.h3: Cycle time, shrinkage and common defects

blocks.text: Cooling usually takes the largest share of the cycle because plastics conduct heat poorly. A thick wall cools much more slowly than a thin wall, so wall thickness controls output more than fill speed does. Pack pressure decides how much shrinkage is compensated while the part is still molten. High pack pressure reduces sink marks but can raise frozen-in stress and warpage.

items: Short shot: incomplete fill; causes include low injection pressure, low melt temperature, cold mould or blocked gate.
Flash: excess plastic at the parting line; causes include too high pack pressure or poor mould closing.
Sink marks: local surface depressions; thick ribs or bosses shrink after the skin freezes.
Weld lines: weak visible lines where two melt fronts meet and do not knit fully.
Warpage: uneven cooling or uneven packing leaves different shrinkage across the part.

blocks.text: Process control sets melt temperature, mould temperature, injection speed, pack pressure and cooling time. The operator should not fix a defect by changing one setting blindly: short shot and flash can both appear when pressure is wrong, but in opposite directions. The examiner often asks for the cycle order and for the reason cooling dominates.

Extrusion uses a screw extruder: pellets fall into a hopper, the rotating screw melts and conveys them along a heated barrel, and the melt is forced through a die. A melt pump, often a gear pump, steadies flow and pressure. The extrudate then passes through a cooling bath or air cooling and is pulled by a haul-off at controlled speed. The product is continuous: pipe, film, sheet, rod, cable insulation or a profile such as a window frame.

Injection moulding and extrusion both use a screw and a melt, but their logic differs. Injection moulding is cyclic and makes discrete parts in a closed mould. Extrusion is continuous and makes a constant cross-section through an open die. A long pipe is therefore an extrusion product, not an injection moulding.

Some syllabi add compression moulding for thermosets. A measured charge of compound is placed in a heated mould cavity. The mould closes and applies pressure, so the charge fills the cavity and cures by chemical cross-linking. After cure, the mould opens and the part is ejected. Compression moulding is cyclic, but it is not extrusion and does not use a rotating screw. Mould design details belong to a later course.

examples.question: An injection moulding cycle has fill 2 s, pack 3 s, cool 15 s and eject 5 s for one cavity. Find the cycle time and the output per hour.
steps: Cycle time t<sub>c</sub> = fill + pack + cool + eject = 2 s + 3 s + 15 s + 5 s = 25 s.
Output per hour N = 3600 s/h ÷ 25 s/part = 144 parts/h.
examples.answer: The cycle time is 25 s, and the output is 144 parts per hour.
examples.check:
fill = 2
pack = 3
cool = 15
eject = 5
cycle = fill + pack + cool + eject
output = 3600 / cycle
print(cycle)
print(int(output))

traps: Calling extrusion a cyclic process that makes discrete parts; extrusion is continuous through a die.
Using only fill time as cycle time and forgetting pack, cool and eject.
Saying a thermoset can be remelted like a thermoplastic; thermosets cure and cannot be remelted.
Confusing short shot with flash: short shot is incomplete fill, flash is excess plastic at the parting line.
Treating viscosity as density; viscosity is resistance to flow, and it falls when melt temperature rises.

quiz.a: A thermoplastic softens on heating and can be remelted. A thermoset cures into a cross-linked network and cannot be remelted.

quiz.q: Name the four stages of the injection moulding cycle in order.
Why does cooling usually dominate injection moulding cycle time?
quiz.a: Plastics have low thermal conductivity, so heat leaves the part slowly. The part must be stiff enough to eject without damage, so cooling time is often longer than fill and pack.

quiz.q: A cycle has fill 1.5 s, pack 2.5 s, cool 12 s and eject 4 s. Find cycle time and output per hour.
A part shows a short shot near the far end of the cavity. Give two likely causes and one suitable correction.
quiz.a: Low injection pressure or low melt temperature can make the melt freeze before filling. Cold mould or a blocked gate can also cause it. Raise melt or mould temperature, increase injection pressure or speed, or clear the gate.

quiz.q: What is melt viscosity, and why does melt temperature matter?
quiz.a: Viscosity is resistance to flow. Higher melt temperature usually lowers viscosity, so the melt fills easier, but too high a temperature can degrade the polymer.

quiz.q: A part has a weld line. Explain the likely cause and give one fix.
quiz.a: Two melt fronts meet after flowing around a core or from two gates, and they do not knit fully. Raise melt or mould temperature, increase injection speed, or move the gate.

quiz.q: A plant must make a 6 m constant-cross-section PVC pipe. Should it use injection moulding or extrusion? Give the reason.
quiz.a: Use extrusion. The pipe has a constant cross-section and is long, so a continuous die and haul-off are natural. Injection moulding is cyclic and would need an impractical long mould.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses multi-cavity hot-runner moulds, co-extrusion, twin-screw compounding and simulation to balance fill, pack and cooling. Recycling and bio-based thermoplastics make melt viscosity and thermal history important again. Search next for polymer rheology, injection moulding simulation and extrusion die design.
